name: Turner Contemporary
summary: Free seafront art gallery by David Chipperfield, named after J. M. W. Turner and his long links with Margate.
description: Turner Contemporary is Margate's flagship art gallery, standing right on the seafront beside the harbour at the edge of the Old Town. It opened on 16 April 2011 in a set of pale, angular buildings designed by the architect David Chipperfield, chosen after an earlier, more ambitious scheme was dropped as too costly. The gallery takes its name from the painter J. M. W. Turner, who went to school in Margate and kept coming back throughout his life, drawn by the light and the skies over the sea here. There is no permanent collection: instead the gallery runs a changing programme of exhibitions of historic and contemporary art, often with a Turner link, along with talks, family activities and events. The big windows look straight out over the water, so even between exhibitions it is worth a visit for the view. Entry is free, which makes it an easy rainy-day stop combined with a walk along the Harbour Arm and the Old Town.
opening_hours: Summer (April-October): Tuesday-Sunday and bank holidays 11am-5pm. Winter (November-March): Wednesday-Sunday and bank holidays 11am-5pm. May close fully or partly between exhibitions (gallery's own visit page, Oct 2026; some older listings say 10am).
dogs: Only guide, hearing and assistance dogs in the galleries; pets are welcome in the café.
accessibility: Step-free access across all floors; large-print guides, sensory bags and audio-described tours; mobility scooters welcome (no e-scooters).
tips: From November the gallery is closed Mondays and Tuesdays. It is about a 15-minute seafront walk from Margate station.

name: Shell Grotto
summary: Mysterious underground passages lined with millions of shells, discovered in 1835 and still unexplained.
description: The Shell Grotto is one of Margate's great oddities: a winding underground passage and chamber whose walls and roof are covered in mosaics made from an estimated 4.6 million seashells, about 2,000 square feet of decoration in all. Most accounts say it was found by chance in 1835, when a man digging on his land broke into it, and it has been open to paying visitors almost ever since, staying in private hands. The passage runs about 21 metres to a rectangular room often called the altar chamber, with a domed rotunda along the way. Nobody knows who made it, when, or why. Theories range from a Georgian or Regency folly to a medieval chalk mine that was later decorated, or links to secret societies, and the debate is part of the fun. The patterns include stars, flowers, hearts and strange symbols. It is Grade I listed. Above ground there is a small museum, shop and café.
opening_hours: Daily 10am-5pm from 21 Oct to 1 Nov (2026 half term); after that Thursday-Sunday 11am-4pm, according to the grotto's own site. Visit Thanet lists Wednesday-Sunday 10am-5pm, so check before going.
price: Adult £6, concession £5, child £2, family £13 (prices on official site, Oct 2026)
tips: It is a short uphill walk from the Old Town. Combine with Margate Caves, a few minutes away on Northdown Road.

name: Dreamland Margate
summary: Historic seafront amusement park, free to enter, home of the Scenic Railway wooden roller coaster.
description: Dreamland sits behind Margate's Main Sands on a site that has been used for seaside entertainment since 1866, when a restaurant and dance hall called the Hall by the Sea opened here. The first rides arrived in 1880, and the Dreamland name dates from 1920, the same year the wooden Scenic Railway roller coaster opened; it is now a listed structure. The park closed in the mid-2000s and its future looked bleak, but after a long local campaign it reopened in June 2015 with a mix of restored vintage rides and newer attractions, and the Scenic Railway ran again from October 2015. Today the park is free to walk into, with rides paid for by wristband, and it also hosts concerts, roller skating and seasonal events in the grounds and the art deco cinema building on the seafront. It is a good place to feel Margate's old holiday-resort character.
address: Hall By The Sea Road, Margate, Kent
opening_hours: 2026 season: weekends and school holidays to the end of October; open every day for October half term, Sat 24 Oct - Sun 1 Nov 2026, roughly 10:30-16:00 (varies by day). Winter opening not confirmed; check the website.
price: Free entry; ride wristbands extra (half price through October 2026, full prices not published on the page I checked).
tips: On Sat 24 Oct 2026 the front doors close at 2pm for a Halloween event; use the Belgrave Road car park entrance. Dreamland car park (400 spaces) is next door.

name: Margate Caves
summary: Old chalk mine turned Victorian attraction, with painted walls, reopened in 2019 with a café and exhibition.
description: Margate Caves are a set of man-made caverns dug into the chalk between the Old Town and Cliftonville, originally as a chalk mine. In 1863 they were opened as a seaside attraction under the invented name of the Vortigern Caves, and the Victorians painted the walls with colourful scenes of soldiers, hunters and pirates, some of which you can still see. The caves stayed popular well into the twentieth century but closed in 2004. A local campaign starting in 2011 brought them back, and they reopened in 2019 with a new visitor centre including a café, shop and exhibition space. The story told on site runs from an Iron Age settlement through the mining years to the modern attraction. Inside it is cool and damp all year, so bring a layer. It pairs well with the Shell Grotto, a few minutes' walk away, for a rainy-day underground tour of Margate.
opening_hours: Wednesday-Sunday 10am-5pm, last entry 4.30pm; daily during half term 24 Oct - 1 Nov (2026).
price: Adult £5, concession £4, child (under 16) £2.50, family (2+2) £12; children 3 and under free (official site, Oct 2026).
tips: Children must be accompanied by an adult. Concessions cover over-60s, students, registered disabled and armed forces.

name: Tudor House
summary: Margate's oldest building, an early 16th-century timber-framed house with a knot garden. Currently outside view only.
description: The Tudor House on King Street is described by Visit Thanet as the oldest building in old Margate, dated to 1525. It is a rare surviving 'transitional' house from the period when hall houses were giving way to more modern layouts, and its early glazed windows and two chimneys were advanced features for their time. The house was restored in 1951 and is Grade II* listed. At the back there is a Tudor-style knot garden with box-hedge squares, and an old malthouse survives on the site, a reminder that barley beer was once made here. The building has been run by volunteers and opened for guided tours in the past, but at the time of writing it is closed until further notice and can only be admired from the outside. It is still worth a short detour on a walk around the Old Town, as it shows how small Margate was before the seaside boom.
opening_hours: Closed until further notice - external viewing only (Visit Thanet, Oct 2026).
tips: The Market Street car park is close by. View it on an Old Town stroll.

name: Margate Old Town
summary: Compact maze of old lanes behind the harbour, full of independent shops, cafés, galleries and small museums.
description: The Old Town is the historic core of Margate, a small grid of narrow streets and squares tucked between the harbour, the Turner Contemporary and the High Street. Before the town became a resort, this was where the fishing and trading community lived, and today it is the liveliest corner of Margate, packed with independent shops, vintage stores, galleries, bars and cafés. Market Place sits at its heart; the Grade II listed former Victorian police station and magistrates' court here houses Margate Museum, which was not open to visitors when this was written. Nearby are the free Crab Museum on Broad Street, the Tudor House on King Street and the Old Kent Market on Fort Hill. The area is easy to explore on foot in an hour or two, and it makes a natural loop with the seafront, the Harbour Arm and the gallery. Many businesses keep shorter hours in winter and early in the week.
address: Market Place and surrounding streets, Margate, Kent
opening_hours: Open streets; shop and café hours vary.
accessibility: Mostly level, but some narrow pavements and cobbled or sloping lanes.
tips: Margate Museum (Market Place) was listed as not currently open to visitors in October 2026.

name: Crab Museum
summary: Quirky free museum all about crabs in Margate Old Town, with a gallery, crab-themed shop and small café-bar.
description: The Crab Museum is one of Margate's more playful attractions: a small, independent museum in the Old Town devoted entirely to crabs. It sits on the upper floor of a building on Broad Street, above the Pie Factory gallery, and mixes real natural history with humour, hand-drawn displays and plenty of crab trivia. The museum has a gallery space, a gift shop selling crab-themed goods and educational zines, and the Crab Café, which serves drinks including alcoholic ones. Entry is free and the museum says it intends to stay that way, relying on donations to keep going, though some special events and performances are ticketed. School and group visits are welcome by arrangement. It is a good short stop for families or anyone exploring the Old Town lanes, and it makes an easy rainy-day add-on to the Turner Contemporary, just a few minutes' walk away.
opening_hours: Friday-Sunday 11am-5pm, last entry 4.30pm; extra days in school holidays (e.g. Wed 28 and Thu 29 Oct 2026).
accessibility: Entry by a flight of stairs with handrail; no wheelchair access at present.

name: Margate Main Sands
summary: Margate's classic sandy town beach opposite the station, with promenade, swing boats and Dreamland behind.
description: Main Sands is the big, gently shelving sandy beach that made Margate a resort, curving between the Harbour Arm and the Nayland Rock end of the seafront. It lies directly opposite Margate railway station, so it is one of the easiest beaches in Kent to reach without a car: the high-speed train from London St Pancras takes around 1 hour 20 minutes. Behind the sand runs a wide promenade with a sea wall, seating and steps down to the beach, part of the town's flood defences. The Round Café beside the Clock Tower sells drinks and snacks, and from Easter to September there is a children's play area with traditional swing boats. Dreamland, the Old Town and the Turner Contemporary are all within a few minutes' walk. The beach held a Blue Flag in 2019. Note the strict summer dog ban; outside the season it is a popular spot for dog walks and winter sunsets over the bay.
address: Marine Terrace / Marine Drive, Margate, Kent
opening_hours: Open access
dogs: Dogs banned on the beach 1 May - 30 September (all day).
accessibility: Promenade is level and paved; steps and slopes to the sand.
tips: Toilets by the Round Café are seasonal (April-September); those near Nayland Rock Shelter open all year. Parking: Dreamland car park (400 spaces) or Mill Lane multi-storey.

name: Margate Harbour Arm
summary: Stone harbour pier beside the Turner Contemporary: an easy walk with wide views over the bay and the town.
description: The Harbour Arm is the curving stone pier that shelters Margate's small harbour, starting next to the Turner Contemporary at the edge of the Old Town. Walking out along it is one of the simplest pleasures in Margate: on one side you look across the harbour to the gallery and the old buildings of the waterfront, on the other you see the long sweep of the Main Sands and the seafront towards Westbrook. At low tide the harbour floor dries out and you can watch birds feeding on the exposed sand and mud. The landward end is marked by the Droit House, the old harbour office building. The pier is a favourite spot for watching the sun go down over the sea, something Turner himself painted many times from Margate. Small venues along the arm open with seasonal hours, so in winter it can be very quiet and exposed; bring a windproof layer.
opening_hours: Open access (individual businesses on the arm keep their own hours).
accessibility: Level stone surface, but uneven in places and exposed to wind and spray.
tips: Best at sunset. Avoid in storms: waves can break over the arm.

name: Walpole Bay Tidal Pool
summary: Huge 1937 sea-water bathing pool on the foreshore, about four acres, refilled by every tide. Free, unsupervised.
description: Walpole Bay Tidal Pool is one of the largest tidal bathing pools in Britain, a walled enclosure on the foreshore at Cliftonville covering about four acres. It was built in 1937, designed by Margate's borough engineer and constructed by the council's own workforce, and was one of two tidal pools made at the time so that people could swim whatever the state of the tide: on this flat coast the low-water mark can be hundreds of metres from the promenade. The walls are made of interlocking concrete blocks, with old tram rails set into them for strength. At low tide you can walk out along the top of the walls; at high tide the sea covers it completely and then refills it as the water drops back. The pool is Grade II listed and is much loved by year-round swimmers. It is free and unstaffed: there is no lifeguard, and no changing rooms, toilets or showers at the pool.
opening_hours: Open access; usable for swimming at mid to low tide.
dogs: Walpole Bay beach: dogs on leads 10am-6pm, 1 May - 30 September.
accessibility: Steep slopes or steps down from the clifftop; walls are slippery with weed.
tips: Check tide times. Wear water shoes: the pool floor and walls are slippery and rocky. No lifeguard.

name: Theatre Royal Margate
summary: Georgian theatre of 1787, said to be the UK's second-oldest working theatre. Closed since 2022 for restoration.
description: Tucked away near Hawley Square, the Theatre Royal was first built in 1787 to entertain the well-off visitors of Georgian Margate, competing with the town's Assembly Rooms. It was remodelled in 1874, turning the Georgian playhouse into the Victorian auditorium that survives today, and it is Grade II* listed. The council describes it as the UK's second-oldest working theatre. It also has a place in theatre history: Sarah Thorne opened a school of acting here in 1885, said to be the first drama school in the country, and the stage designer Edward Gordon Craig was among its pupils. The building closed in April 2022 and was added to the Theatres Trust's at-risk register back in 2018. Thanet District Council has secured millions of pounds of Town Deal funding to restore it and is looking for a long-term operator, so for now you can only see the outside. It is a pleasant stop on a walk around the Georgian squares behind the Old Town.
opening_hours: Closed to the public since April 2022; restoration planned (no reopening date confirmed by the council).
tips: Outside view only. Hawley Square next door has fine Georgian houses.

name: Winter Gardens
summary: Edwardian clifftop concert hall of 1911, closed since 2022 and being refurbished with a reopening planned for 2027.
description: The Winter Gardens is Margate's big clifftop entertainment venue, set into the slope above the sea on Fort Crescent, east of the Old Town. It opened in August 1911 and for more than a century hosted concerts, variety shows, dances and comedy, with a main hall holding around 2,100 people. The venue closed in 2022 when its operator handed the lease back to Thanet District Council because of a backlog of repairs. Westwood One, which runs the Granville Theatre in Ramsgate, has since been chosen to take it on, and a planning application published in May 2026 set out a major refurbishment with extra bars, a rooftop bar and café, a drama school, a nursery, a larger main hall for about 3,000 people and a new smaller performance space. In August 2026 the reopening was announced for March 2027. Until then you can see the building from the outside and enjoy the views from the clifftop gardens around it.
opening_hours: Closed for refurbishment; reopening announced for March 2027 (Aug 2026 reports).
tips: Outside view only for now. Combine with a clifftop walk east towards the Lido and Walpole Bay.

name: Cliftonville Lido & Clifton Baths
summary: Art deco lido sign above early 19th-century sea baths cut into the chalk cliff. Mostly derelict; view from outside.
description: On the seafront at Cliftonville, the tall LIDO sign marks one of the most atmospheric relics of Margate's resort past. The story starts with the Clifton Baths, dug into the chalk cliff between 1824 and 1828 and among the earliest surviving sea-bathing buildings in the country; their remains are Grade II listed. In 1926 John Henry Iles, the man behind Dreamland, developed an art deco lido complex over the old baths, with sun terraces, cafés, bars and a pool stretching towards the sea. The pool was filled with sand after storm damage in the late 1970s, other parts of the complex limped on until the early 2000s, and the site has largely stood derelict since. Local volunteers have been clearing and caring for parts of it, and in 2025 plots of the land were put up for sale, so its future remains uncertain. It is a striking sight on a coastal walk between the Winter Gardens and Walpole Bay.
address: Ethelbert Terrace / Ethelbert Crescent, Cliftonville, Margate, Kent
opening_hours: Not open as an attraction; view from the promenade and clifftop.
tips: Best seen from the lower promenade at low tide.

name: Botany Bay
summary: Thanet's most photographed beach: soft sand, white chalk cliffs and stacks, rock pools and a smuggling past.
description: Botany Bay is the northernmost of Broadstairs' bays and probably the most dramatic beach on the Isle of Thanet. A sandy cove about 200 metres long, it is framed by white chalk cliffs and free-standing chalk stacks that stand out on the sand at low tide, with small coves, rock pools and the chance of a fossil between them. Thanet has one of the longest continuous stretches of coastal chalk in Britain, and this is where it is most spectacular. The bay also has a smuggling story: in 1769 the smuggler Joss Snelling and his gang were caught landing contraband here by a revenue patrol, and a bloody fight followed in which Snelling escaped but many of his men did not. Access is by steps or a steep slope from the clifftop, and at low tide you can walk round to Kingsgate Bay. There is a kiosk for drinks and snacks, deckchair hire and seasonal toilets. The sand is sometimes cut off by the rising tide, so keep an eye on the water.
opening_hours: Open access
price: Free; free on-street parking on Botany Road
accessibility: Steps or a steep slope only; very soft sand.
tips: Go at low tide to see the stacks and walk to Kingsgate Bay, but check tide times so you are not cut off. Seasonal toilets from late March, 8am-6.45pm.

name: Kingsgate Bay
summary: Small secluded cove below Kingsgate Castle with some of Thanet's best sea caves. Dogs allowed all year.
description: Kingsgate Bay is a small, sheltered sandy cove about 150 metres wide, tucked between Botany Bay and Joss Bay and overlooked by the battlements of Kingsgate Castle on the clifftop. It is reached by a steep flight of steps, which keeps it quieter than its neighbours. The bay is known for its sea caves, among the best examples on the Thanet coast and once used by smugglers; the chalk here is of national importance for its caves and wildlife. Some sand is left even at high tide, but the sea can cut off both ends, so if you walk round from Botany Bay at low tide, watch the time. There is no lifeguard and there are no toilets on the beach; the nearest facilities and RNLI lifeguards are at Botany Bay and Joss Bay, about a 15-minute walk away. Unlike most Thanet beaches, dogs are welcome here all year, and the Captain Digby pub is on the clifftop above.
opening_hours: Open access
accessibility: Steep steps only.
tips: Check tides before exploring the caves; the beach can be cut off at both ends. No toilets.

name: Kingsgate Castle
summary: Mock-medieval clifftop castle built around 1760 as Lord Holland's stables, now private flats. View from outside.
description: Perched on the cliff above Kingsgate Bay, Kingsgate Castle looks like a medieval fortress but is in fact an eighteenth-century folly. It was built for Henry Fox, the first Lord Holland, around the 1760s as the stable block for Holland House, his seaside retirement home nearby, and was styled to resemble an Edwardian castle in Wales. Lord Holland filled the area with follies and mock ruins, and after his family sold the estate much of it decayed; the big round tower is the main survivor of the original building. In the late nineteenth century John Lubbock, the first Lord Avebury, rebuilt and enlarged the castle. After a sale in 1922 it became a fashionable hotel until the 1950s, and it was then converted into private flats. It is a listed building and not open to the public, but it makes a fine sight from the beach below or from the coastal path between Botany Bay and Joss Bay.
address: Kingsgate Avenue area, Kingsgate, Broadstairs, Kent
opening_hours: Private residences - external viewing only.
tips: Best viewed from Kingsgate Bay beach or the Viking Coastal Trail on the clifftop.

name: Joss Bay
summary: Wide sandy bay below chalk cliffs, Thanet's surfing beach, with a large car park, café and surf school.
description: Joss Bay is a broad sandy bay surrounded by white chalk cliffs on the coast between Kingsgate and North Foreland. It is said to take its name from the smuggler Joss Snelling, who worked this coast in the eighteenth century, though which name came first is still debated. The bay faces the open sea and is the best-known surfing beach on the Isle of Thanet; a surf school here rents out wetsuits, boards and kayaks. With a large car park right above the sand, a seasonal café, deckchair hire and a children's play area in summer, it is one of the easiest family beaches in the area. Sand remains at high tide, but both ends of the bay are cut off when the sea comes in, so keep an eye on the tide if you wander round towards the next coves. North Foreland Lighthouse stands on the headland just to the south.
opening_hours: Open access
price: Free; pay-and-display car park (charges 1 April - 31 October)
accessibility: Slope or steps from the car park to the sand.
tips: Seasonal toilets from late March, 8am-6.55pm. Out of season the car park is free.

name: North Foreland Lighthouse
summary: Historic clifftop lighthouse, the last in Britain to be automated (1998). Seen from outside; cottages to rent.
description: North Foreland Lighthouse stands on the headland at the north-eastern tip of Kent, guarding the approaches to the Thames and the treacherous Goodwin Sands. A light is said to have been shown here as early as 1499; the first true lighthouse was a timber tower of 1636 that burned down in 1683, and the core of the present tower dates from 1691. Trinity House took it over in the nineteenth century. Its most famous moment came in 1998, when it became the last of Trinity House's lighthouses to be automated, ending centuries of resident keepers; the Duke of Edinburgh, then Master of Trinity House, attended the ceremony. The light is now monitored remotely from Harwich in Essex. The tower is Grade II listed and is not normally open for visits, but it is a handsome sight from the road, and the keepers' cottages beside it can be rented as holiday accommodation.
opening_hours: Working lighthouse - not regularly open to the public (public access not confirmed).
tips: Combine with Joss Bay, a short walk to the north.

name: Stone Bay
summary: Quiet chalk-cliff bay north of Viking Bay with beach huts and morning sun; fully covered at high tide.
description: Stone Bay lies just north of the town centre of Broadstairs, beyond Bleak House, and is a calmer alternative to the busy main beach. White chalk cliffs surround it and part of the bay is protected by a concrete sea wall and promenade, with rows of beach huts in use from April to September. Facing east, it catches the best of the sunshine in the early part of the day. It held a Blue Flag in 2019. The important thing to know is that at high tide the bay is completely covered by the sea, so plan your visit around low tide. Access is down steps from Eastern Esplanade; vehicles use a steep slope with a hairpin bend. The toilets here open from April to September, while those at Viking Bay, a short walk along the sea wall, are open all year, and Viking Bay also has plenty of cafés and restaurants.
opening_hours: Open access; beach covered at high tide.
accessibility: Steps from Eastern Esplanade; steep slope for vehicles.
tips: Go at low tide - there is no sand at high water.

name: Viking Bay
summary: Broadstairs' horseshoe main beach, with the little harbour, tidal pool, cafés and Dickens sights above.
description: Viking Bay is the main beach of Broadstairs, a sheltered horseshoe of sand beneath the town with the small harbour and pier on one side and a tidal pool on the other. It got its name after 1949, when the replica Viking ship Hugin landed here after sailing from Denmark; the ship now stands at Pegwell Bay. Plenty of sand remains even at high tide, which makes it reliable for families. A wooden boardwalk runs from Harbour Street, past the Pavilion, to the first steps down from the clifftop promenade. On summer weekends cafés and an ice-cream kiosk open on the beach, and there is a children's play area. Above the bay you can see Bleak House on the cliff, and the Dickens House Museum and Morelli's ice-cream parlour are on Victoria Parade behind it. Toilets are open all year. Note the full dog ban in summer.
address: Harbour Street / Victoria Parade, Broadstairs, Kent
opening_hours: Open access
price: Free; nearby car parks at Albion Street and Harbour Street
dogs: Dogs banned at all times 1 May - 30 September.
accessibility: Boardwalk from Harbour Street; otherwise steps from the clifftop promenade.
tips: Arrive early on summer weekends: the car parks are small (81 and 69 spaces).

name: Bleak House
summary: Clifftop house above Viking Bay where Charles Dickens spent summers and worked on David Copperfield. Private.
description: Bleak House is the castellated house on the cliff above Viking Bay, the most famous of Broadstairs' many links with Charles Dickens. Built around 1801 and originally called Fort House, it was the novelist's favourite holiday home: he rented it for summer stays and is said to have planned and written parts of David Copperfield here, as well as his essay on Broadstairs, Our English Watering-Place. The house was much enlarged in 1901 and was renamed Bleak House in the early twentieth century after Dickens's novel. In recent years it served as a guest house and wedding venue, but it has been a private home again since 2021 and is not open to the public. You can still enjoy the view of its turrets from the beach and the harbour, and it is a stop on the Broadstairs Dickens town trail along with the Dickens House Museum on Victoria Parade.
opening_hours: Private home - external viewing only.
tips: Visit Thanet publishes a free Dickens town trail for Broadstairs.

name: Dickens House Museum
summary: Seafront cottage that inspired Betsey Trotwood's home in David Copperfield, with Dickens letters and prints.
description: This small museum on Victoria Parade overlooks Viking Bay and celebrates Charles Dickens's long association with Broadstairs, where he holidayed between 1837 and 1862. The house was home to Mary Pearson Strong, a local woman whom Dickens knew and who is thought to have inspired the formidable Betsey Trotwood in David Copperfield; although Dickens set Miss Trotwood's cottage in Dover, his description matches this house. The museum occupies the ground and first floors, with period rooms including a parlour modelled on Betsey Trotwood's, Victorian costume, and collections of Dickens's letters and belongings, early editions and serial parts, and illustrations by Phiz and other artists of his books. There is also a display on what Dickens wrote about Broadstairs, and a small gift shop. The museum is run by Thanet District Council and staffed by volunteers. It opens only in the summer season, on afternoons.
opening_hours: 2026 season: Wednesday 1 April - Sunday 1 November, Wednesday-Sunday 1pm-4.30pm (last entry 4pm). Closed in winter.
accessibility: Two floors with 14 stairs and no lift; ground floor accessible, ramp alternative to the entrance step. Accessible toilets about 160 m away at the Bandstand.
tips: Last chance in 2026 is Sunday 1 November. A concession may apply if you can only visit the ground floor.

name: Morelli's
summary: Family-run retro Italian ice-cream parlour on the seafront since 1932, with pink booths and a jukebox.
description: Morelli's is a Broadstairs institution: an Italian ice-cream parlour and coffee bar on Victoria Parade, looking straight out over Viking Bay. The Morelli family business dates back to 1907 and its Broadstairs parlour opened in 1932; it is still owned and run by the family. Much of the charm is the interior, which has kept a wonderfully retro look with a soda fountain, jukebox, formica tables and pink leatherette booths, refurbished in its classic style decades ago. Alongside freshly made gelato, with vegan options, it serves coffee, tea, soft drinks, Prosecco, cakes, pastries and Italian savouries. Mint choc chip and pistachio are said to be the favourite flavours. Sitting in a booth with a sundae after a walk on the beach is one of the quintessential Broadstairs experiences, and it is right next to the Dickens House Museum.
opening_hours: Monday-Friday 8am-5pm, weekends 8am-6pm (Visit Thanet listing; longer hours in summer have been listed elsewhere - check).
tips: Busy on summer afternoons; mornings are quieter for coffee.

name: Crampton Tower Museum
summary: Small volunteer museum in a flint water tower by the station, about engineer Thomas Russell Crampton and transport.
description: Crampton Tower Museum is a small, family-friendly museum partly housed in a flint tower right next to Broadstairs railway station. The tower once formed part of the town's first public water supply, and the museum celebrates Thomas Russell Crampton, the Victorian engineer born in Broadstairs who was behind it. Crampton is best known for his railway locomotive designs, but he also worked on gasworks, waterworks and submarine telegraph cables, and was the first to lay a working telegraph cable under the English Channel. The displays cover his life and work alongside local and transport history, from railway models to items about old Broadstairs. The museum is run by volunteers and opens on a few afternoons a week in the summer season. The tower itself is reached by a winding staircase with no lift, but the rest of the building is wheelchair accessible.
opening_hours: 2026 season: Friday 3 April - Sunday 1 November, Friday-Sunday and bank holiday Mondays 2pm-4.30pm (last entry 4pm). Closed in winter.
accessibility: Tower has a winding staircase with no lift; rest of the building wheelchair accessible; accessible toilets. Accessible parking behind Broadstairs Library, about 100 m.
tips: Right by Broadstairs station - easy by train from Birchington.

name: Ramsgate Royal Harbour
summary: Britain's only harbour with the 'Royal' title, granted by George IV in 1821; marina, piers and waterfront cafés.
description: Ramsgate's harbour is the heart of the town and carries a unique distinction: it is the only harbour in the United Kingdom entitled to call itself a Royal Harbour. The title was granted by King George IV in 1821, after he sailed from Ramsgate to Hanover and was charmed by the welcome he received; an obelisk of 1823 on the East Pier commemorates the visit. Work on the harbour began in 1749, and several of the great engineers of the day were involved, among them John Smeaton, who built sluices and the cross wall in the 1770s and the advanced pier in the 1780s and 1790s. Today the inner and outer basins are a busy marina lined by arches housing cafés, bars and restaurants, with fishing boats, yachts and the occasional historic vessel moored up. Walk out along the piers for views back to the cliffs and the town, and look for the Clock House at the head of the harbour. It was designated a Heritage Harbour in 2024.
address: Harbour Parade / Military Road, Ramsgate, Kent
opening_hours: Open access
accessibility: Harbour-side roads and promenades are mostly level.
tips: Visit Ramsgate publishes a Royal Harbour Trail leaflet.

name: Ramsgate Tunnels
summary: Guided tours of an 1863 railway tunnel and the WWII air-raid shelter network carved under Ramsgate.
description: Beneath the cliffs of Ramsgate lies one of Britain's most extensive civilian air-raid shelter networks, now open for guided tours. The story starts with a mainline railway tunnel of 1863, about two-thirds of a mile long, which once carried trains down to a station on the seafront. In 1936 a narrow-gauge railway was run through it to the beach, and in the late 1930s the town built a deep-shelter system connected to it; the air-raid precaution tunnels opened on 1 June 1939 and were designed to shelter up to 60,000 people. During the Second World War some families whose homes were bombed lived down here for long periods. Tours lead you through the old railway tunnel and part of the shelter network, telling the story of the town at war. Booking ahead is recommended. It is cool underground all year, so bring a layer.
opening_hours: October: Mon-Fri 10am-2pm, Sat-Sun 10am-4pm. 1 Nov - 31 Mar: Wednesday-Monday 10am-2pm (closed Tuesdays, Christmas and New Year). May-Sep: daily 10am-4pm. Pre-booking recommended.
tips: There are no toilets in the tunnels; use the Bathing Station toilets nearby beforehand. Tickets are sold online.

name: The Grange (Pugin's house)
summary: A. W. N. Pugin's own Gothic Revival home of 1843-44, restored by the Landmark Trust. Open on set open days.
description: The Grange is the house that Augustus Welby Northmore Pugin, the architect behind the interiors of the Houses of Parliament and a leading figure of the Gothic Revival, designed and built for himself and his family in 1843-44 on the West Cliff at Ramsgate. He chose the spot for its view of the sea, which he loved, and next door he built St Augustine's Church. The Grange is Grade I listed. After years of decline it was rescued from demolition by the Landmark Trust in 1997 and carefully restored to look as it did in Pugin's time, with richly coloured wallpapers, tiles and woodwork. It is now a Landmark holiday let sleeping up to eight people, so it is not open daily, but the Trust holds free open days several times a year, including in June and during Heritage Open Days in September, and visits can be arranged by appointment. The upper floors are reached by steep stairs.
opening_hours: Holiday let; open only on Landmark Trust open days (2026: 5-8 June and 11-14 September) and by appointment.
accessibility: Steep stairs to upper floors.
tips: Check the Landmark Trust for the next open days; combine with St Augustine's Church next door.

name: St Augustine's Church & Shrine
summary: Pugin's own Gothic Revival church (1846-52), where he is buried; national shrine of St Augustine since 2012.
description: St Augustine's is the church Augustus Pugin built, largely at his own expense, next to his home, The Grange, on Ramsgate's West Cliff. Work began in the mid-1840s and continued until his death in 1852, and many regard it as his most personal building, designed exactly as he wanted with no client to please. Pugin is buried here in a vault beneath the chantry chapel he designed, under a tomb with an effigy by his son Edward, alongside members of his family. The church is Grade I listed. In March 2012 it was made the official shrine of St Augustine of Canterbury, who landed in Thanet in 597 to bring Christianity to the English, and it holds a relic of the saint. The former schoolroom became a visitor and education centre in 2017, telling the story of Pugin and the church. It is still a working Catholic church with regular services, so please be respectful.
opening_hours: Shrine and visitor centre: 12.30pm-3.30pm daily except Tuesday and Sunday (Visit Thanet, Oct 2026).
tips: Pugin Week in early September brings talks, tours and open days around the church and The Grange.

name: The Clock House (Ramsgate Maritime Museum)
summary: Listed harbour building, former Maritime Museum, under restoration; reopening targeted for autumn 2026.
description: The Clock House is a handsome Grade II* listed stone building at the head of Ramsgate Royal Harbour, and for many years it was home to the town's Maritime Museum, telling the story of the harbour, its ships, wrecks and lifeboats. Thanet District Council took the building back in 2023, and since August 2025 it has been undergoing a major restoration and extension, funded through the government regeneration money for Ramsgate. The works include new exhibition spaces, removal of the containers that stood beside it, and a café extension. The council has said it will reopen once construction is finished, with an autumn 2026 target, but that the full museum displays will take longer and that parts of the building may first open as temporary 'meanwhile' spaces for heritage activities. The museum collection is in safe storage in the meantime. Even while closed, the building is a landmark on any walk around the harbour.
address: Pier Yard, Royal Harbour, Ramsgate, Kent
opening_hours: Closed for restoration; reopening targeted for autumn 2026, no date announced as of Oct 2026.
tips: Check Thanet District Council's Clock House page for the reopening date.

name: Ramsgate Main Sands
summary: Sandy town beach just east of the Royal Harbour, below the East Cliff, good for early sun.
description: Ramsgate Main Sands is the town's central beach, a stretch of sand about 250 metres long immediately east of the Royal Harbour, below the East Cliff and the grand old Royal Victoria Pavilion. Facing south-east, it is one of the best spots on the Thanet coast for early morning sunshine. A pedestrian promenade runs the length of the sand, with kiosks, cafés and restaurants within a short walk, and the entrance to the Ramsgate Tunnels is on Marina Esplanade just behind. Toilets at East Pier Yard are open all year, while the Bathing Station on Marina Esplanade opens in summer only. It is a convenient beach if you arrive by train or bus and want to combine a swim or paddle with the harbour, the tunnels and lunch in town. Dogs are banned at the harbour end of the beach in summer.
opening_hours: Open access
dogs: Dog ban at the harbour end, 1 May - 30 September.
accessibility: Level promenade along the beach.
tips: Combine with the Ramsgate Tunnels tour next door.

name: Viking Ship Hugin
summary: Replica Viking longship that sailed from Denmark in 1949, displayed on the clifftop at Pegwell Bay.
description: On the clifftop above Pegwell Bay stands the Hugin, a full-size replica of a Viking longship modelled on the ninth-century Gokstad ship. It was built in Denmark and sailed across the North Sea in 1949 by a crew of 53 Danes, almost all amateurs, to mark 1,500 years since the legendary landing of the Anglo-Saxon leaders Hengist and Horsa at nearby Ebbsfleet. The ship came ashore at Broadstairs, where the main beach was renamed Viking Bay in its honour, and it was then given by the Daily Mail to Ramsgate and Broadstairs and moved to its present spot overlooking the bay. Thanet District Council restored it in 2005 with European funding. You can only view it from outside its fence, and it is covered up in winter to protect it from the weather. A picnic site and café are close by, and the coastal path runs past towards Pegwell Bay Country Park.
opening_hours: External viewing only, any time; the ship is covered over the winter months.
tips: In winter the ship is under covers, so summer is the best time to see it.

name: Pegwell Bay Country Park
summary: Coastal nature reserve on the Stour estuary, on the site of the old hoverport, with saltmarsh views and birds.
description: Pegwell Bay Country Park lies on the shore of the wide, shallow bay where the River Stour meets the sea between Ramsgate and Sandwich. It is part of the Sandwich and Pegwell Bay National Nature Reserve, about 615 hectares of mudflats, saltmarsh, sand dunes and grassland, managed by Kent Wildlife Trust and important for wading birds and wildfowl. The park itself is built partly on the concrete apron of the former hoverport, from which Hoverlloyd ran cross-Channel hovercraft services until the early 1980s, and the bay's cliffs are of real geological interest. Paths lead along the shore with big views across the estuary, and with binoculars you may pick out the seals that use the sandbanks of the Stour. The Viking ship Hugin stands on the clifftop just to the east. There is a pay-and-display car park, seasonal toilets and a kiosk near the ship.
opening_hours: Reserve open 8.30am-7pm, or dusk if earlier.
accessibility: Mostly flat paths and grass; height barrier at the car park entrance.
tips: Seasonal toilets (April to mid-September). Bring binoculars for the birds on the mudflats at low tide.

name: Spitfire & Hurricane Memorial Museum
summary: Free museum at the old RAF Manston airfield with a real Spitfire and Hurricane, plus a café and simulators.
description: This volunteer-run museum stands on the edge of the former RAF Manston airfield, which played a front-line role in the Battle of Britain. Its centrepieces are two genuine wartime fighters displayed indoors: a Supermarine Spitfire Mk XVI and a Hawker Hurricane Mk IIc. Around them are displays of artefacts about the airfield and about life in and around Ramsgate during the Second World War. Entry is free, and the museum is entirely self-funded, so donations are very welcome. For an extra charge you can book a Spitfire flight experience or an Avro Lancaster flight simulator session. The Merlin Café on site makes it an easy half-day out, and the RAF Manston History Museum is right next door for more aviation history. The whole site is step-free with accessible parking and toilets, and it is only a short drive from Birchington.
address: The Memorial Museum, Manston Road, Manston, Ramsgate, Kent
opening_hours: Daily 10am-4pm (Visit Thanet, Oct 2026). Some listings say closed Mondays in winter and over Christmas/New Year - check before visiting.
price: Free (donations welcome). Spitfire flight experience £30/30 min; Lancaster simulator £75/30 min (Mon-Wed, phone to book).
dogs: Trained assistance dogs on leads only.
accessibility: Step-free throughout; manual doors with volunteer help; one wheelchair to borrow; accessible toilet by the café; two accessible bays in the free car park.
tips: Free parking. Combine with the RAF Manston History Museum next door.

name: RAF Manston History Museum
summary: Volunteer museum on the history of Manston airfield from 1916, with a Canberra, Vulcan and Victor cockpit.
description: The RAF Manston History Museum tells the story of the airfield at Manston from its beginnings in 1916, through two world wars and the Cold War, to search-and-rescue work and its later life as a civil airport. Run by volunteers, it holds a large collection of aircraft and artefacts, including an English Electric Canberra, an Avro Vulcan cockpit section and the cockpit of a Handley Page Victor tanker, along with vehicles, uniforms, models and memorabilia. There is a gift shop and the NAAFI café for refreshments. It sits right next to the Spitfire and Hurricane Memorial Museum, so the two are easily combined for a half-day of aviation history, ideal on a grey day. Opening depends on volunteer availability, so it is worth checking the website before setting off.
opening_hours: Summer: daily 10am-4pm (last entry 3.15pm). Winter: Mon-Fri 10am-3pm (last entry 2.15pm), Sat-Sun 10am-4pm (last entry 3.15pm). Subject to volunteer availability.
price: Adult £7, concession £6, child (under 16) £3.50, carer £4, family (2+up to 4) £20, under-5s free (official site, Oct 2026).
dogs: Guide, hearing and assistance dogs welcome.
accessibility: Ramped entrance; about 90% of the museum is wheelchair accessible; two floors with about 9 steps and no lift; accessible toilets and parking.
tips: Annual pass available (adult £24).

name: Minster Abbey
summary: Benedictine convent on a 7th-century monastic site, with buildings from 1027; free tours on Saturday mornings.
description: Minster Abbey, in the village of Minster just south of Manston, is one of the oldest religious sites in England. The first monastery here was founded around 670, and the present buildings go back to 1027; parts were destroyed at the Reformation, but fine medieval ranges survive and Visit Thanet describes it as possibly the oldest inhabited house in England. Uniquely, it is the only pre-Reformation monastery in England that is again home to a religious community: a group of Benedictine nuns came here from Germany in 1937 and the sisters still live and pray on site today. Visitors are welcome in the chapel, which is open daily for prayer, and the nuns run guided tours of the historic buildings and grounds. There is also a small exhibition area and tearoom. Entry is free. It is a peaceful place, so please be quiet near the community's areas.
opening_hours: Guided tours Saturdays 11am-12 noon all year, other times by appointment. Chapel open daily for prayer. Tearoom/exhibition Mon-Fri 10am-4pm (entrance on Bedlam Court Lane); hours vary in winter - ring ahead.
dogs: Pets and assistance dogs welcome (Visit Thanet).
accessibility: Step-free on the ground floor; accessible toilets and parking near the entrance; hearing loop in the chapel.
tips: Minster station is close by on the Ramsgate-Canterbury line.

name: Richborough Roman Fort & Amphitheatre
summary: English Heritage Roman fort where the AD 43 invasion likely came ashore; huge walls, museum and amphitheatre.
description: Richborough, just north of Sandwich, is one of the most important Roman sites in Britain. Known to the Romans as Rutupiae, it is thought to be where the invasion force of AD 43 came ashore, and defensive ditches from that time can still be traced. It grew into a major port and the gateway to the province, the start of Watling Street, and around AD 85 a colossal triumphal arch about 25 metres high was built here to mark the conquest. In the late third century the Romans built a Saxon Shore fort, whose massive stone walls, in places still several metres high, are the most impressive thing you see today. The sea that once lapped the fort has long gone, as the Wantsum Channel silted up, leaving the site a couple of miles inland. There is a small museum with finds, a kids' trail, and a short walk to the earthworks of the amphitheatre, which held around 5,000 people.
opening_hours: Open daily 10am-5pm, last entry 4.30pm (English Heritage, late Oct 2026). Winter opening from November not confirmed - check before going.
price: English Heritage admission (prices not shown on the pages I could read); 15% off booking online by midnight the day before; free for EH members.
tips: Closed on very windy days (e.g. 23 Oct 2026). Combine with Sandwich, 2 miles away.

name: Sandwich (Cinque Port town)
summary: Remarkably intact medieval Cinque Port: timber-framed streets, the River Stour quay, Fisher Gate and the Barbican.
description: Sandwich, about 20 minutes' drive south of Birchington, is one of the best-preserved medieval towns in England. It was one of the original Cinque Ports, and its wealth came from the sea until the harbour silted up and left the town two miles inland on the River Stour. That decline froze its streets in time: Strand Street is said to have more timber-framed buildings than any other street in England. Along the quay you will find the Fisher Gate, the only one of the town's medieval gates still standing, dating from the 1380s and later enlarged, and the Barbican, a fourteenth-century gatehouse beside the bridge where tolls were collected until 1977. Other sights include St Clement's Church with its fine Norman tower, the Guildhall of 1579, and St Bartholomew's Hospital, founded in 1190 for pilgrims heading to Canterbury. The Sandwich Medieval Centre on the quay demonstrates crafts. Richborough Roman Fort is just north of town.
opening_hours: Town streets open access; individual sights vary.
accessibility: Historic streets are narrow with uneven pavements in places.
tips: Sandwich has a railway station on the line from Ramsgate. Walk the quay and the old town walls path.

name: Sandwich Guildhall
summary: Brick Guildhall of 1579 in the Cattle Market, long home to the town's museum and its rare Magna Carta copy.
description: The Guildhall stands on the Cattle Market in the centre of Sandwich and has been the seat of local government for more than four centuries. It was built in 1579, with later alterations, and is a Grade II* listed building. Inside is an atmospheric old courtroom, and the building long housed the Sandwich Guildhall Museum on the town's history. Its most famous treasures are original copies of Magna Carta and the Charter of the Forest dating from 1300; the Magna Carta's significance was only realised in 2015, when it made national news. Sandwich Town Council took over the building in 2018 and uses it as its offices and meeting place. Because arrangements for viewing the museum and the charters have changed over the years, check with the town council before making a special trip. Even from outside, it is a natural starting point for a stroll around the town.
opening_hours: Not confirmed - contact Sandwich Town Council for museum/charter viewing times.

name: Canterbury Cathedral
summary: Mother church of the Church of England, founded in 597; site of Becket's murder and part of a World Heritage Site.
description: Canterbury Cathedral is one of the most important churches in Christendom and the obvious highlight of a day trip to Canterbury, about half an hour from Birchington by train or car. It was founded in 597 by St Augustine, sent from Rome to convert the Anglo-Saxons after landing in Thanet, and it is the seat of the Archbishop of Canterbury. In 1170 Archbishop Thomas Becket was murdered in the north-west transept by knights of Henry II, and his shrine in the Trinity Chapel, built in 1180-84, made Canterbury one of Europe's great pilgrimage destinations until the shrine was destroyed in 1538. Highlights include the soaring nave, the magnificent medieval stained glass, the tomb of Edward the Black Prince, the great central Bell Harry Tower and the Romanesque crypt, which survived a fire in 1174. Together with St Augustine's Abbey and St Martin's Church, it forms a UNESCO World Heritage Site designated in 1988. Choral Evensong is sung daily.
address: Cathedral House, 11 The Precincts, Canterbury, Kent
opening_hours: Mon-Sat 10am-5pm (last admission 4pm); Sun 11.30am-5pm, church from 12.30pm (last admission 4pm). Subject to change.
price: Adult £18 (October-March), £19.50 (April-September); under-18s free with a paying adult ('Kids Go Free'); services free to attend.
dogs: Assistance dogs welcome; other dogs only in the Refectory garden in café hours (spring/summer), on a short lead.
tips: Book online for fast-track entry. Evensong at 5.30pm daily is free. Café (The Lounge) 10am-4pm.

name: Westgate Towers
summary: England's largest surviving medieval city gate (c.1380), a former jail with a small museum and rooftop view.
description: The Westgate is the great twin-towered gateway at the western end of Canterbury's main street, and the largest surviving medieval city gate in England. It was rebuilt around 1379-80 under Archbishop Simon Sudbury on the site of an older gate, and it stands about 18 metres tall, the last survivor of the city's seven medieval gates. From the fifteenth to the nineteenth century the gate served as the city's prison, and you can still see grim reminders of that use. Today the towers house a small museum, escape rooms and a bar, and the climb to the top rewards you with views over the rooftops towards the cathedral. Steep, narrow stone staircases make it unsuitable for wheelchairs, buggies or anyone with limited mobility. Next to the gate, the riverside Westgate Gardens along the Great Stour are a lovely spot for a picnic or to watch punts go by.
accessibility: Steep, narrow stone stairs; not suitable for wheelchairs or prams.
tips: Canterbury West station is a two-minute walk away.

name: Canterbury Roman Museum
summary: Underground museum built around a Roman town-house mosaic floor found after the 1942 Blitz, with a silver hoard.
description: Canterbury Roman Museum lies below today's street level, built around the remains of a Roman town house whose mosaic floors were revealed after a German bombing raid flattened this part of the city in 1942. The mosaics are still in their original position and are the heart of the visit. Around them the museum tells the story of Durovernum Cantiacorum, as Roman Canterbury was called, with everyday objects such as household gods, glass, silver spoons, tools and tiles, military finds including cavalry harness and swords, and the Canterbury Treasure, a late Roman silver hoard. Reconstructions of a Roman house kitchen and a market street with shops help bring it to life, and children can handle replica artefacts and try making mosaics. The site first opened to the public in 1946 and was refurbished as the Roman Museum in 1994. It is only a short walk from the cathedral gate.
opening_hours: Monday-Sunday 10am-5pm, last admission 4.30pm (official site, 2026).
price: Adult £11, concession £9, child (5-15) £5.50, under-5s free (official site, 2026).
accessibility: Visitor lift available (occasionally out of service).
tips: Booking ahead is recommended. Canterbury residents with My Canterbury membership get free entry.

name: St Augustine's Abbey
summary: English Heritage ruins of the abbey founded by St Augustine, later a Tudor palace; part of the World Heritage Site.
description: Just outside Canterbury's city walls lie the ruins of St Augustine's Abbey, founded by St Augustine himself soon after his mission arrived from Rome in 597. It was one of the most important monasteries in Anglo-Saxon England and the burial place of early archbishops and kings of Kent. The Normans rebuilt it on a grand scale, and after the Dissolution part of it was turned into a royal palace for Henry VIII. What remains today are extensive low walls and foundations spread across a peaceful lawn, with information panels and a site museum explaining the Saxon monastery, the Norman rebuilding and the Tudor palace, plus games for children. Together with the cathedral and St Martin's Church it forms Canterbury's UNESCO World Heritage Site. It is a quieter and more contemplative stop than the cathedral, only a few minutes' walk east of the cathedral precincts.
opening_hours: Open daily 10am-5pm, last entry 4.30pm (English Heritage, late Oct 2026). Winter hours not confirmed.
price: English Heritage admission (price not confirmed); free for EH members.
tips: Walk on a few minutes to St Martin's Church to complete the World Heritage trio.

name: St Martin's Church, Canterbury
summary: Said to be the oldest church in the English-speaking world still in use; Queen Bertha's chapel before 597.
description: St Martin's is a small, unassuming church on a hillside east of Canterbury's centre, yet it is described as the oldest church building in the English-speaking world still in regular use. Before St Augustine arrived in 597, this was the private chapel of Queen Bertha, the Christian Frankish wife of King Æthelberht of Kent, who was allowed to keep her faith and worshipped in a converted Romano-British building on this site. Look closely at the walls and you will see reused Roman bricks and tiles, and a blocked doorway in the chancel may date from Bertha's time. Scholars still debate whether the building was already a church in the Roman period. It is a Grade I listed building and forms part of the Canterbury World Heritage Site along with the cathedral and St Augustine's Abbey. It remains a working Church of England parish church, so opening for visitors depends on volunteers.
tips: Check the parish website for visiting times before walking out.

name: The Beaney House of Art & Knowledge
summary: Canterbury's Victorian museum, library and art gallery on the High Street, reopened in 2012 after refurbishment.
description: The Beaney is Canterbury's central museum, library and art gallery, housed in a grand Victorian building on the High Street. It opened in 1899 as the Beaney Institute, funded largely by a bequest from Dr James George Beaney, a Canterbury-born surgeon who made his fortune in Australia, with help from the city council. After a major refurbishment it reopened in 2012. Inside you will find a free public library with local studies material, galleries of fine and decorative art, and museum displays drawn from the city's collections. The art collection is especially known for paintings by local artists Thomas Sidney Cooper and his son William, famous for their pastoral scenes with cattle and sheep, and it includes a portrait by Van Dyck bought in 2004. The building is Grade II listed and its decorated façade is worth a look in itself. It makes a good indoor stop between the cathedral and the Westgate.

name: Reculver Towers & Roman Fort
summary: Twin medieval church towers on the clifftop inside a Roman fort, a famous landmark for sailors. Free.
description: The twin towers of Reculver are one of the great landmarks of the north Kent coast, visible for miles along the shore and only a few miles west of Birchington along the Viking Coastal Trail. They stand within the remains of Regulbium, a Roman fort that became part of the chain of Saxon Shore defences. In 669 an Anglo-Saxon minster was founded inside the fort, which later became the parish church of St Mary, and the two towers were added in the twelfth century. As the sea ate away at the soft cliffs, much of the fort and the church were lost; the church was largely demolished in the early nineteenth century, but the towers were kept as a navigation mark for shipping. Today they are looked after by English Heritage and are free to visit from outside during daylight, with interior access to the North Tower on selected days in summer. Around them, Reculver Country Park offers clifftop grassland and coastal walks.
opening_hours: Exterior viewable during daylight hours; North Tower interior on selected days April-October.
price: Free; charged public car park next to the site (not English Heritage).
tips: A classic cycle or walk from Birchington along the Viking Coastal Trail past Minnis Bay (about 5 km).

name: Herne Bay Pier
summary: Seaside pier whose long Victorian neck was wrecked by storms in 1978; the old pier head still stands far out at sea.
description: Herne Bay has had a pier since 1832, when a timber pier more than 1,100 metres long was built, designed by Thomas Rhodes, an assistant of Thomas Telford. It was replaced in stages, and the third pier, opened in 1899, stretched about 1,154 metres out to sea so that steamers could call at any tide; at the time it was one of the longest in the country. The twentieth century was unkind: the pavilion burned down in 1970, and storms in 1978 and 1979 smashed the central section, which was dismantled in 1980. What survives is a short stub at the shore end, now home to kiosks run by the Pier Trust for local businesses, and, most strikingly, the old pier head, standing alone in the sea far offshore. It is too solid to demolish and carries a navigation light. The promenade, the Victorian clock tower and the seafront gardens make Herne Bay a pleasant traditional seaside stop on the way to Whitstable.
opening_hours: Pier shore end open access; kiosk hours vary.
accessibility: Promenade and pier stub are level.
tips: The isolated pier head is best seen from the end of the pier or the seafront at sunset.

name: Whitstable Harbour & seafront
summary: Working fishing harbour famous for oysters, with seafood stalls, shingle beaches and the 'Street' spit at low tide.
description: Whitstable is the classic day trip along the coast west of Herne Bay, best known for its oysters and its lively, arty seafront. The harbour was opened in 1832 by the Canterbury and Whitstable Railway company so that coal could be moved straight from ships onto trains, and today it is still a working harbour for fishing, fish processing and cargo, ringed by seafood stalls, fishmongers and huts selling local catch. Whitstable oysters have Protected Geographical Indication status; native oyster stocks fell in the twentieth century and Pacific oysters are now farmed on the foreshore. Every July a nine-day Oyster Festival begins with a parade and the 'landing of the catch'. East of the harbour, at low tide, a natural shingle spit called The Street runs about 800 metres out to sea and you can walk along it. Above it the grassy Tankerton Slopes and the eighteenth-century Whitstable Castle, now a community venue with gardens, complete the walk.
opening_hours: Harbour area open access; stall and shop hours vary.
accessibility: Harbour and promenade mostly level; beaches are shingle.
tips: Check tide tables if you want to walk out on The Street - it covers quickly on the rising tide.

name: Tankerton Slopes & The Street
summary: Grassy slopes with beach huts and rare Hog's Fennel, overlooking a shingle spit you can walk at low tide.
description: Tankerton is the eastern end of Whitstable, and its grassy Slopes are one of the nicest spots on this coast for a picnic or a stroll. Lines of colourful beach huts sit along the top, and the slopes look out over the sea towards the Isle of Sheppey. They are also of national importance for wildlife: Tankerton Slopes hold the largest English population of the rare Hog's Fennel plant, a food plant of the scarce Fisher's estuarine moth. Below, the shingle spit known as The Street runs about 800 metres straight out to sea. It is exposed at low tide, when you can walk out along it with water on both sides, and it is the remnant of an old river valley drowned by the sea. Whitstable Castle, built as an octagonal tower in 1789 and later enlarged into a manor house, sits nearby at the boundary with Tankerton, surrounded by public gardens.
opening_hours: Open access
accessibility: Slopes are steep grass; level path along the top on Marine Parade.
tips: Walk The Street only on a falling or low tide and come back well before the water returns.

name: Wingham Wildlife Park
summary: Family zoo between Canterbury and Sandwich with primates, big cats, a dinosaur zoo and soft play. Open all year.
description: Wingham Wildlife Park is a popular family zoo in the countryside between Canterbury and Sandwich, about half an hour's drive from Birchington. It opened in 1986 as a bird park and was renamed in the 1990s as its collection grew; today it covers around 25 acres and holds hundreds of animals of many species. Primates are a highlight, with chimpanzees, Bornean orangutans, gibbons, mandrills, several kinds of monkey and lemurs among them. Since 2016 a permanent dinosaur zoo has added around 30 life-size animatronic dinosaurs, a children's fossil pit and local fossil displays. There is also an indoor soft play area, which is useful on wet days. The park is open every day except Christmas Day. Because some animals roam free on site, dogs, including guide dogs, are not allowed, and children cannot enter without an adult.
opening_hours: Winter (October-March) 9am-4pm; summer (April-September) 9am-6pm; last admission one hour before closing. Open daily except 25 December.
price: Adult £25, senior/student £23, child (2-15) £22, family (2+2) £88, under-2s free (official site, Oct 2026).
dogs: No dogs at all, including guide dogs (free-roaming animals).
tips: Pre-booking is encouraged. Annual membership available.

name: Howletts Wild Animal Park
summary: Aspinall Foundation park near Canterbury with famous gorilla families and the UK's largest African elephant herd.
description: Howletts, in parkland at Bekesbourne just south-east of Canterbury, began as John Aspinall's private zoo in 1957 and opened to the public in 1975. It is now run by the Aspinall Foundation, a conservation charity that also runs Port Lympne near Hythe. The park is known for keeping animals in large, naturalistic family groups, and it is famous above all for its western lowland gorillas, with some of the biggest gorilla family groups anywhere; the Foundation has returned more than 75 gorillas to the wild in Africa. Howletts is also home to the largest herd of African elephants in the UK, along with leopards, tigers, many kinds of monkey and other rare species, set across around 90 acres. Paths are mostly flat tarmac with gentle slopes, making it manageable with buggies and wheelchairs, and there are places to eat on site. Allow most of a day.
opening_hours: Daily 10am-5pm until 1 November 2026; winter mostly 10am-4pm (Fri-Sun only 4 Jan-12 Feb and 22 Feb-25 Mar 2027). Last entry 2 hours before closing.
dogs: Assistance dogs only under the park's assistance dog policy (general dog policy not confirmed).
accessibility: Mostly flat tarmac paths with gentle slopes; wheelchairs for hire at the Gatehouse; accessible toilets and parking.
tips: Book online; ticket prices are on the Aspinall Foundation booking page.

name: Dover Castle
summary: Huge English Heritage castle above the white cliffs: Henry II's Great Tower, a Roman lighthouse and WWII tunnels.
description: Dover Castle crowns the white cliffs above the Channel port, about 45 minutes' drive from Birchington, and is one of the largest and most impressive castles in England. Its story spans two thousand years. Within the walls stands one of only three Roman lighthouses that survive anywhere, next to the Saxon church of St Mary in Castro. The mighty Great Tower was built for Henry II between 1179 and 1188, and inside its rooms are dressed to show the splendour of his court; a separate exhibition tells the story of the great siege of 1216-17. Deep in the cliffs is a network of tunnels used in the Second World War as a command centre and underground hospital; from here Admiral Ramsay directed Operation Dynamo, the Dunkirk evacuation of 1940. The Underground Hospital is open, though the Operation Dynamo tour was closed for maintenance in October 2026. There are two cafés, a siege-themed play area and sweeping views over the harbour and towards France.
opening_hours: Open daily 10am-5pm, last entry 4pm (English Heritage, late Oct 2026). Reduced winter opening from November not confirmed - check before going.
price: English Heritage timed tickets (2026 prices not shown on the pages I could read); up to 15% off booking online; 20% off arriving by public transport or bike; free for EH members.
accessibility: Underground Hospital and tunnels are not accessible by wheelchair or mobility scooter.
tips: Closed in very high winds (e.g. 23 Oct 2026). A WWI gun is fired on Saturdays at 12.30pm and 1.30pm.
